source_text: Factum est enim animal rationale, mortale, capax virtutis et vitii, quod posset ex concessa sibi possibilitate vel servare Dei mandata, vel transgredi, vel magisterio naturali conservare ius humanae societatis, liberumque haberet alterutram velle partem, in quo peccati et iustitiae summa est. Nam cum aliquid secundum virtutem indigentibus, aut de misericordiae fontibus, aut de iustitiae immulget uberibus; hoc operatur foris iam ipsa iustitia, quam intus voluntas sancta concepit et peperit.
pass_a_gloss: For a rational animal was made, mortal, capable of virtue and of vice, which could from the possibility conceded to it either keep the commands of God, or transgress, or by a natural teaching preserve the right of human society, and would have it free to will either part, in which is the sum of sin and of justice. For when something according to virtue he milks for those in need, either from the fountains of mercy or from the udders of justice; this already works outside, the justice itself, which inside a holy will conceived and bore.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere

pass_b_english: For the human being was made a rational, mortal living being, capable of virtue and vice. Through the capacity granted to him, he could either keep God's commands or transgress them, or by nature's teaching preserve the law of human fellowship. He was free to will either alternative; in this lies the substance of sin and justice. For when he draws something according to virtue for those in need, either from the springs of mercy or from the breasts of justice, it is justice itself working outwardly, which a holy will conceived and brought forth within.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
